about: Mock cases for the kb search suite. All content is invented; shapes mirror observed usage (counts in references/refreshing-cases.md).

classes.acronym: A short upper-case term; should find its glossary row or the note that defines it.
classes.expansion: The long form of an acronym; should find the glossary row or a note that uses the term.
classes.identifier: A code symbol (class, function, constant, flag); should find its definition or the note about it.
classes.file-name: Part of a file name typed from memory.
classes.error-string: An exact error or alert text pasted from a log or pager.
classes.guid: A correlation id pasted from a log.
classes.work-item: A work item number in #NNNN form.
classes.title: A few words of a note's title.
classes.config-key: A configuration key or environment variable, often with escaped dots.
classes.request-question: A person's question to an agent, paraphrased so it shares few words with the answer.
classes.request-task: A person's instruction to an agent; the answer is the note and/or code the work depends on.

queries.q: Ops at the south site are complaining again that drivers roll in an hour ahead of their booking and clog the yard lane. I'm fairly sure we made a call on this over the summer. Dig up what we decided and summarise it in three sentences. Don't change any code yet.

Two things. First, I'm writing the quarterly reliability review in reviews/2026-q3-reliability.md and need a paragraph on last month's incident where two carriers were both confirmed for the same bay at the same hour. Find out what actually caused it and what we changed in the booking code afterwards, and link whatever write-up exists. Second, the table of contents in that review is out of order, fix it while you're there. Keep the tone neutral, no blame, and commit each change separately so I can review them one at a time.
How much do we refund our biggest accounts when a load arrives late, and does the amount depend on account size?

Finance pinged me: a handful of shippers say they were billed twice for one load back in August. Before I reply, find out whether we already know the cause and whether it's been fixed. Add a line to docs/finance-faq.md once you know, but ask me before pushing anything.

Sorry, long one. The pager went off twice overnight for the pile of messages our consumers gave up on, and it's still climbing this morning. I was on call last week too so I'm a bit fried. Context: we moved to one parked-message bucket per consumer back in May, so I'm not even sure which consumer is the problem yet, and the replay tool the platform team is building isn't ready. I don't want you to replay or purge anything. What I need is the steps on-call is supposed to take first when that page fires, in order, with the commands, so I can work through them myself. If there are thresholds that tell me whether to wake someone up, include those too. Separately, check whether the on-call rota in the team calendar is right for next week, I think Sam and I got swapped. Keep the answer short, plain text, no tables.

I'm putting together slides for Thursday's ops review. Which of our sites kept drivers waiting on the premises longest between July and the end of September? I need the numbers per site, not just a ranking, and keep the wording plain because the audience isn't technical.

We have a new engineer joining the routing team on Monday and onboarding/routing-week-one.md is pretty thin. Add a short section explaining why we moved away from re-calling carrier APIs on a fixed timetable, what we do now instead, and what problem that solved. One paragraph, plain language, and link to the original decision rather than copying it. Also bump the last-reviewed date at the top of the page. Commit when done, don't push.
Callers are seeing the proxy cut their connections before any reply arrives. Draft a short checklist on-call can follow tonight.

For Friday's status update I need three bullets:
- where the experiment on taking more bookings than we have bays currently stands
- what last month's numbers showed
- what is blocking the next step
Keep each bullet under twenty words and don't invent numbers.

The weekend job that copies production data into pre-prod failed again on Saturday. The masking step on customer fields ran past its window and the whole thing got killed. I looked at pipelines/weekend-copy.yml and the timeout there looks fine to me. Figure out what we're supposed to do when masking runs long and how to get it through next weekend. Also, unrelated, the dashboard link in the team channel topic is broken, find the right one. Ask me before rerunning anything.

Ops asked what happens in the booking service when a driver shows up ahead of time and every bay is occupied. Point me at the function that makes that decision and explain the branch in two or three sentences, I'll forward it to them. No code changes.

I need to know how long the route planner waits between attempts when a carrier API doesn't respond, and whether that wait is randomised or fixed. I already checked config/application.yaml and only found the overall timeout there. Reply with the class name and the formula, nothing else.
Find where we work out time on site for a truck that was never scanned leaving. Just the function, please.

Picking up from yesterday's chat. We agreed in the routing sync to stop the planner's carrier re-attempts from all firing in lockstep after an outage, so please make the change now. Context: last time a big carrier came back after twenty minutes down, every queued call hit them in the same second and they throttled us for an hour. I sketched some notes in scratch/carrier-outage-notes.md but treat them as rough, they're not the decision. What I want:
1. spread the wait between attempts using the approach we settled on, not the old fixed steps
2. keep the current maximum number of attempts exactly as it is
3. update the unit tests so they don't depend on exact wait values
Run the build and tests locally before you commit, and keep the commit message short. Don't touch the timeout settings, that's a separate conversation with the carrier team next week. If anything about the agreed approach is unclear, stop and ask me rather than guessing.

When a dispatcher tries to book a bay that another carrier already has, our API sends back a vague error and they end up phoning the ops desk. Change the response so it says which carrier holds the booking and until what time. Update the API spec to match, and keep the HTTP status code as it is so existing clients don't break. While you're in there you'll notice the error messages mix British and American spelling; leave that alone, I'll raise a separate ticket. Commit when the tests pass.
Long-haul arrival predictions ignore the rest stops drivers are legally required to take. Account for them, and add a test.

Gate arrival events get redelivered almost immediately after a consumer fails, so a flaky downstream gets hammered over and over. Make the gaps between redeliveries longer. The old doc about gate events describes the previous behaviour, ignore it. Keep the change small and tell me what you changed in one or two lines.

I'm writing a design note for the gateway and want to cite the general pattern for stopping lots of clients from all hammering a server the instant it recovers. Find what I wrote on that in my own notes and give me a two-line summary I can paste in.
Find the list of paperwork I need to gather for this year's filing with the revenue office. I can't remember where I put it.

Quick home one before I start work: when did I last clear the limescale out of the coffee machine, and is it due again? It isn't in projects/grinder-swap.md, I checked. After that, get back to the index migration we started yesterday.

I'm prepping for Wednesday's study group. Make me eight to ten review cards on how a cluster of replicas chooses which node is in charge, and what happens when that node dies partway through a write. Question on one side, answer on the other, one idea per card. Only use my own notes, not the internet. At the end, remind me to book the meeting room, and keep your reply itself short because I'll paste the cards straight into the app.

We keep getting double submissions from the booking form when people's connections drop and the app resends. Before I touch that code, write me a short checklist, based on my own notes, for making an API call safe to send more than once. Keep it under ten items, no table, and say which items need a database change. Unrelated: the README in the form project still mentions the old build command, flag it but don't fix it yet. I'll pick this up after lunch.
